newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seen at odds with IMF over strategy.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seen at odds with IMF over strategy.

text.p: The new Pakistani government's growth-oriented approach to economic problems may lead to friction with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), according to a research report on Thursday.
An IMF mission is in Islamabad for a two-week review of the economy prior to a decision on whether to release the next $122 million tranche of a standby loan due at the end of March.
The report by ABN AMRO Bank N.V. said Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's move to freeze utility prices until June and his preference for a supply-side strategy might not win IMF favour.
A supply side strategy would imply slashing interest rates and taxes to boost output and exports -- at the risk of fuelling inflation, widening the fiscal deficit and increasing imports.

"Since the policy prescriptions advocated by a supply side strategy will go against the austerity measures promised by the caretaker government, future interaction with the IMF is bound to be strained," the report said.

A caretaker government promised in December to cut the budget gap to four percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96 to meet IMF conditions for resumption of the stalled standby loan.
"The growth dividend (a popular supply side argument) is a medium-term strategy which is unlikely to meet any targets agreed to with the IMF," the ABN AMRO report said.
Soon after winning the February 3 election, Sharif announced that fuel prices and utility charges would not be increased before the end of the fiscal 1996/97.

The report said the prime minister's action, at variance with the caretaker government's promises to bring fuel and utility prices in line with world prices, would require government subsidies and increase distortions in the economy.
"Perhaps it was felt that the rise in prices could create resentment and unrest, with political costs which outweigh the possible problems with the IMF," the report said.
The consumer price index increased 13.83 percent year-on-year in February, with inflation largely driven by prices of essential food items and imported fuel.
ABN AMRO said the government, eager to curb food prices, planned to import more wheat and sugar and to curtail rice exports, despite the risk of increasing the trade deficit.
"It is hoped that by increasing local supply it would be possible to break the upward trend in prices," it said.
Pakistan's trade deficit fell to a provisional $2.324 billion in the first eight months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from $2.361 billion in the year-ago period.
Renewed investor confidence has brought higher private inflows, boosting Pakistan's cash reserves to $1.001 billion on March 1 from $850 million on February 20.
But ABN AMRO said Pakistan could not alienate itself from the IMF while its external sector remained under pressure.
"Given the magnitude of recent inflows...the fear is that if IMF conditions are dismissed as being too stringent, the government may break talks with the IMF," the report said.
"Nawaz Sharif has the unenviable task of resolving Pakistan's short-term concerns without jeopardising our relationship with the international agencies," it added.
